opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't really see it as competition, at least not in the way people usually mean it. The world-model problem is enormous. We're trying to build systems that understand how the physical world evolves: how objects move, how forces act, how an action leads to a consequence. No single team is going to solve that alone. It's a bit like the early days of deep learning, when many groups were pushing in parallel and everyone benefited from each other's progress.

At NVIDIA, our position is also a little different. We're a platform company. When we work on world foundation models, a big part of the goal is to enable the ecosystem: robotics companies, autonomous-driving teams, researchers in universities. That's why we've tried to be open, releasing models, tokenizers, and data-curation tools so people can build on top of them. If another team takes our model, post-trains it for their robot, and does something amazing, that's a success for us. It means physical AI is moving forward, and physical AI needs a lot of compute, so it's good for NVIDIA too.

Of course, there's healthy pressure. When I see a great result from another lab, a video model with better physical consistency or a clever way to make it interactive, it pushes us to think harder. But I see that as the field learning together. We read their papers, they read ours.

What I care about most is whether, a few years from now, robots can actually learn safely and efficiently in simulation built from these world models, instead of only in the real world. If we get there, it won't matter much who was first on a particular benchmark. It'll matter that the community collectively made it happen.

r001.rationale: The response says the problem is enormous and no single team will solve it alone, but it does not state that a world model alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It calls another team’s post-training NVIDIA’s model for a robot and achieving something amazing a success, but does not say the resulting model is superior and open source.

r003.rationale: The response says strong results from other labs push NVIDIA to think harder and describes the field learning together, conveying mutual challenge as a driver of progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as competition in the way people usually mean. World models are still so early. If you look at the whole field, nobody has really solved it yet. We don't have a model that truly understands physics, that can simulate the world consistently over long horizons, that an engineer can trust to train a robot or an autonomous vehicle in. So when I see other teams working on this, I mostly feel that the problem is getting more attention, and that is good for everyone.

At NVIDIA, our goal with Cosmos is a little different from some of the other groups. We are not trying to build a product that competes for consumer attention. We are trying to build a foundation for physical AI. Robotics companies, autonomous driving companies, they need huge amounts of data about the physical world, and the real world is expensive and slow to collect from. A world model lets you generate that data, lets you test policies in simulation, lets you evaluate before you deploy. So our users are developers, and we open the models so they can build on them. That shapes how we think about others doing similar work. If someone else releases a strong model, developers benefit, and that ecosystem is what we care about.

I also think the different teams are actually betting on different things. Some are focused on video generation quality, on making beautiful clips. Some are focused on interactive games. We are focused on physical accuracy, on controllability, on things like multi-view consistency for a car, or precise action conditioning for a robot arm. These are different objectives, and the field is big enough that you learn from each other. When another lab publishes something good, we read it carefully, and I am sure they read ours.

And frankly, having spent many years in research, I have seen this pattern before. In the GAN era, in the early days of image generation, there were many groups racing, and the result was that the whole area moved much faster. Competition pushes you to be honest about where your model is weak. That is healthy. What I would worry about more is if nobody else cared about world models. That would mean we were wrong about the direction.

r001.rationale: The response says world models have not yet solved key problems and can help generate data and test policies, but it does not state that a world model alone is insufficient to solve Physical AI problems.

r002.rationale: It says developers benefit when another team releases a strong model and that NVIDIA opens models for developers. It does not say another team could use NVIDIA’s work to build a superior open-source model.

r003.rationale: The response says competition pushes teams to recognize weaknesses and helped the field move faster, describing teams challenging one another as a driver of progress.

astra-6.text: I think competition is healthy, but I don’t see it as a zero-sum game. World models are a very broad area, and there’s still a lot we need to figure out. Different teams will make different bets, and we can learn from one another. From our perspective at NVIDIA, success also means enabling other people to build. So if another team takes something we’ve developed and pushes it further, I see that as a positive outcome. We can compete on ideas while still helping the whole field move forward.

r001.rationale: The response calls world models a broad area with much left to figure out, but does not say a world model alone is insufficient for solving Physical AI problems.

r002.rationale: It says another team pushing NVIDIA’s work further would be positive, but does not specify that the resulting model is superior and open source or that this benefits the Physical AI ecosystem.

r003.rationale: The response describes competition and learning from one another, but does not identify teams challenging each other with higher standards as a driver of progress in Physical AI.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s natural for teams working on world models to see one another as competitors. But I’d rather focus on what we can learn from each other. There are still many hard problems to solve, and different teams will take different approaches. If our work gives others something useful to build on—or motivates them to do something better—that’s a positive outcome. For me, the focus is on doing good research and making these models more useful.

r001.rationale: The response mentions making models more useful, but does not say that a world model alone is insufficient to solve Physical AI problems.

r002.rationale: It calls others building on NVIDIA’s work or doing better a positive outcome, but does not specify a superior open-source model or benefit to the broader Physical AI ecosystem.

r003.rationale: It describes teams as competitors and says they may motivate better work, but does not identify mutual challenges to higher standards as a mechanism for continued Physical AI progress.
